extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_short: logical classification of names and things
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and classify kinds of names and the kinds of things they denote (feelings, substances, attributes), and clarify distinctions important to logical analysis (e.g., sensation vs perception, univocal vs equivocal, substance as substratum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is relative when, over and above the object which it denotes, it implies in its signification the existence of another object, also deriving a denomination from the same fact which is the ground of the first name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: a name is relative when, being the name of one thing, its signification cannot be explained without mentioning another; or cannot be employed in discourse to have meaning unless the name of some other thing be either expressed or understood. Example: 'father' and 'son' connote the same series of events but as attributes of different correlates (fundamentum relationis). Note that attributes expressed by relative names would be swept away if only a single object existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal vs æquivocal names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal when applied in the same sense to all things of which it can be predicated; it is æquivocal (ambiguous) when predicated in different senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous words are effectively different words that happen to coincide in sound; e.g., 'file' (tool) vs 'file' (line of soldiers) are two words accidentally coinciding. Use awareness of sense to avoid fallacious reasoning from ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical (metaphorical) use of names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name used analogically or metaphorically is predicated of two things not univocally but in somewhat similar, derived significations, one primary and the other secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'brilliant' applied to light (primary) and to an achievement (secondary). A common fallacy is to treat metaphorical usage as literal, arguing from the metaphor as if the senses were identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proposition is discourse which affirms or denies something of some other thing; nothing but a Proposition can be an object of belief or of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions require two things: the subject and what is affirmed or denied (predicate) — these are the signified items of the two names joined by a copula. Understanding what all names signify gives knowledge of what can be affirmed or denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration of namable things (categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: All things capable of being predicates or of having anything predicated of them can be enumerated (e.g., classical Categories list: Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Action, Passion, Where, When, Position, Habit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Aristotelian categories are criticized as redundant and defective: some items omitted, others repeated under different heads; they tend to conflate substances and attributes and neglect states of consciousness. A sound classification should analyze the rationale behind common distinctions and include sensations and other states of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling / State of consciousness (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Feeling or State of consciousness is everything of which the mind is conscious; the genus includes Sensation, Emotion, Thought, and Volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In popular language 'feeling' is often restricted; philosophically it covers sensations, emotions, and thoughts (including mental images, beliefs). Distinguish thoughts (states of mind) from objects of thought (external things). Imaginary objects are not thoughts themselves but objects of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: sensation vs object vs attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sensation is distinct from the object which causes it and from the attribute (e.g., whiteness) ascribed to that object; language often fails to give single-word names for sensations apart from objects and attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We name sensations by reference to the object or attribute (e.g., 'the sensation of white' or 'color'); some sensations (like sounds) more readily have independent names because they can occur without a perceptible object. Awareness of this distinction is important for precise analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: sensation vs bodily states (organs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate the sensation itself (a state of mind) from the state of bodily organs which precedes the sensation and constitutes the physical agency producing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophically there is no foundation for dividing feelings into 'bodily' and 'mental'—sensations are states of mind occasioned by bodily states. The bodily phenomenon (retina, optic nerve) is different from the conscious sensation. Confusing these leads to conceptual muddle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as recognition (intuitive belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception, as distinguished by many writers, consists in recognition of an external object as the cause of a sensation; it is an act of the mind and amounts to an intuitive belief that an external cause exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These perceptions are classed among feelings or states of mind for logical purposes. The author refrains from settling metaphysical questions about their legitimacy; laws of intuition belong to psychology/metaphysics, not logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volitions and actions (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volitions (acts of the will) are active states of mind; an action consists of a volition followed by an effect — the volition and its consequent physical effect together constitute an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many relative names connote actions (past, present, possible future); examples include sovereign/subject, physician/patient, mortgagor/mortgagee. Recognize actions as temporally/causally composite when analyzing connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance vs Attribute (grammatical/ontological guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logicians distinguish substances and attributes partly by grammatical usage: an attribute is 'of' something (would cease if its bearer ceased), whereas a substance is said to be self-existent and need not be followed by 'of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grammatical test is inadequate by itself (what is meant by 'of' is unclear and attributes and substances interdepend). A deeper metaphysical account separates bodies and minds and considers their relations to attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body/substance as external cause of sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: A body may be defined as the external cause to which we ascribe our sensations: a conception of a body consists in a number of sensations habitually occurring together (a complex idea) and the inference to an external cause (substratum or matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical controversy (e.g., Berkeley, Idealists) challenges whether substratum is necessary: some argue objects are only sensations ordered by laws; others hold belief in matter is intuitive. Kant concurs that all we know of objects are sensations and their order (phenomena), while the thing-in-itself remains unknowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ambiguous words and choice of terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many fundamental terms (e.g., Thing, Being, Entity, Essence) are ambiguous or have drifted in meaning, the writer will employ whichever term is least likely to mislead in context and will not rigidly confine usage to a single sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When precise terms are lacking, occasional improper use of a term may be justified to call up a helpful association. Logic should exercise care in using vague language so as to convey precise meaning; awareness of the defects of available words is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for including feelings in classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings (including sensations, emotions, thoughts, volitions) should be accounted among realities and included in any comprehensive enumeration of things capable of being named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that prior taxonomies (e.g., Aristotle's) wrongly excluded or miscategorized feelings/states of consciousness; a satisfactory logical classification must treat them explicitly rather than subsuming them under action/passivity without analysis.
